statement:
In adults in a pooled analysis of six case-control studies (2,159 people with lung cancer and 2,985 controls; four of the six studies unpublished) and in Swedish male military conscripts (49,321 at the start, 44,257 in the cannabis analysis) followed for 40 years, as described by the National Academies committee (a narrative review; the pooled analysis and the cohort were not read here, so every figure below is second-hand), evidence is insufficient to say whether smoking cannabis, compared with not smoking cannabis, changes the incidence of lung cancer.

In the pooled analysis, habitual cannabis smoking (at least 1 joint-year) against non-habitual (under 1 joint-year, including never) gave an odds ratio of 0.96 (95% CI 0.66–1.38), and 1.03 (0.51–2.08) among people who did not smoke tobacco; for adenocarcinoma alone the odds ratios were 1.73 (0.75–4.00) for more than 1 joint a day and 1.74 (0.85–3.56) for more than 10 joint-years, not significant. The committee says risk rose with duration and intensity without becoming significant. In the Swedish cohort, men who reported using cannabis more than 50 times at conscription had a hazard ratio of 2.12 (1.08–4.14) for lung cancer against men who reported never using it, adjusted for tobacco, alcohol, respiratory conditions and socioeconomic status at conscription; the committee says studies in an epidemiologic review that are not in the pooled analysis indicate an increased risk. No absolute risks are given in the committee's account.

The committee graded the evidence 'moderate evidence of no statistical association' between cannabis smoking and the incidence of lung cancer (its wording and its judgment; under it sit the pooled case-control analysis and, in its discussion, the cohort and the review). The editors read 'no statistical association' here as not statistically significant in a pooled estimate whose interval does not exclude an odds ratio of 1.38 (a 38% rise) or, among people who did not smoke tobacco, of 2.08, with a cohort pointing up; it is not a finding that smoking cannabis does not raise the risk, and the chapter's highlights go further than its numbered conclusion. A 2018 commentary sets the committee's wording beside a WHO statement (the WHO report was not read) that a cannabis and tobacco mix may increase cancer risk and that the effect of cannabis alone is unknown.

Not measured and limits, as the committee names them: the pooled analysis could not account for differences in smoking technique or in the cannabis smoked, had few people with heavy long-term smoking (imprecise estimates) and relied on self-report without biological confirmation; in the cohort, cannabis and tobacco use after conscription were not followed, its authors did not know whether participants mixed tobacco and cannabis, and the self-reports were not anonymous. The committee adds that cancers have a long incubation period that needs long observation, that cannabis smoke, like tobacco smoke, contains carcinogens, that cannabis use has been associated with cigarette smoking (to which 28.6% of US cancer deaths in 2014 have been attributed, in a study it cites), and that replication is needed because exposures are changing and many associations rest on single studies. No source read compares smoking cannabis with other ways of taking it.

Funding as printed: the committee's report was sponsored by US federal agencies and health foundations, with no cannabis or tobacco industry sponsor listed; the funding of the pooled analysis and of the cohort is not given in the committee's account and is not known here. Certainty: very low. Status: mixed.
plain: A 2017 report by a National Academies committee graded the evidence on smoking cannabis and lung cancer as 'moderate evidence of no statistical association'. It mostly rested on a combined analysis of six studies that compared people with lung cancer with people without it, which found no clear difference between people who smoked cannabis habitually and people who did not; the results were also compatible with up to about 38% higher odds of lung cancer. A long study of Swedish men found about twice the rate of lung cancer in men who had said, when called up for military service, that they had used cannabis more than 50 times, but it did not follow what they smoked later in life. So the evidence cannot show either that smoking cannabis raises the risk of lung cancer or that it does not, and none of these studies can show cause. The committee notes that cannabis use has been associated with cigarette smoking, to which more than a quarter of US cancer deaths in 2014 have been attributed in a study it cites.
population: Adults in a pooled analysis of six case-control studies (2,159 people with lung cancer, 2,985 controls; four studies unpublished) and men in a Swedish cohort of military conscripts (49,321 at the start, 44,257 in the cannabis analysis) followed 40 years, as described by the National Academies committee
exposure: Smoking cannabis, self-reported: habitual (at least 1 joint-year) in the pooled analysis; more than 50 uses reported at conscription in the Swedish cohort (technique, product strength and any tobacco mixed in not accounted for)
comparator: Non-habitual cannabis smoking (under 1 joint-year, including never) in the pooled analysis, also within people who did not smoke tobacco; never using cannabis in the Swedish cohort
outcome: Incidence of lung cancer (adenocarcinoma analysed separately in the pooled analysis)
magnitude: Pooled analysis of 6 case-control studies (2,159 cases, 2,985 controls; committee's account): habitual against non-habitual cannabis smoking OR 0.96 (95% CI 0.66–1.38); among people who did not smoke tobacco OR 1.03 (0.51–2.08); adenocarcinoma only: more than 1 joint a day OR 1.73 (0.75–4.00), more than 10 joint-years OR 1.74 (0.85–3.56), not significant. Swedish conscript cohort (40 years; 44,257 in the analysis): more than 50 uses at conscription against never, HR 2.12 (1.08–4.14), adjusted for tobacco, alcohol, respiratory conditions and socioeconomic status at conscription. No absolute risks given. Committee's grade (its wording): moderate evidence of no statistical association.

evidence.locator: Chapter 5 › Lung Cancer › Systematic Reviews, 1st paragraph; Discussion of Findings, 1st paragraph; Footnote 1
evidence.extracted: Pooled analysis of six case-control studies, four unpublished (2,159 people with lung cancer, 2,985 controls), in the International Lung Cancer Consortium (Zhang et al., 2015): habitual against non-habitual cannabis smoking, odds ratio 0.96 (95% CI 0.66 to 1.38); among people who did not smoke tobacco 1.03 (0.51 to 2.08). Habitual means at least 1 joint-year; non-habitual under 1 joint-year, including people who never used cannabis; not smoking tobacco means under 100 cigarettes in a lifetime or the cut-offs of the pooled studies. Adenocarcinoma only: more than 1 joint a day OR 1.73 (0.75 to 4.00); more than 10 joint-years OR 1.74 (0.85 to 3.56), described by the pooled analysis's authors as suggestive but not significant. The committee adds that risk rose with duration and intensity, but even people with the heaviest and longest smoking were not at significantly greater risk than people who smoked non-habitually.

evidence.locator: Chapter 5 › Lung Cancer › Primary Literature, 1st paragraph; Discussion of Findings, 1st paragraph; Footnote 2
evidence.extracted: Epidemiologic review (Huang et al., 2015; no meta-analysis) of six lung cancer studies, including the pooled analysis and two of its studies. Of the three others, two were set aside by the committee because the pooled analysis's authors described limits (inadequate control of tobacco use, possible reporting bias); the third, a cohort of 49,321 Swedish male military conscripts followed 40 years (44,257 in the cannabis analysis; Callaghan et al., 2013), found a hazard ratio of 2.12 (95% CI 1.08 to 4.14) for more than 50 uses at conscription against never, adjusted for tobacco, alcohol, respiratory conditions and socioeconomic status at conscription. The committee says the studies in the review but not in the pooled analysis indicate an increased risk. No absolute risks are given. The cohort paper itself was not read.

evidence.extracted: Limits of the lung cancer evidence as the committee states them: the pooled analysis could not account for differences in smoking technique or in the cannabis smoked, had too few people with heavy long-term smoking for precise estimates, and relied on self-report without biological validation; in the Swedish cohort detailed cannabis and tobacco use before and after baseline was lacking, tobacco and cannabis were not accounted for during the 40-year follow-up, its authors did not know whether participants mixed tobacco and cannabis, and self-reports were not anonymous.

evidence.locator: Chapter 5 › Lung Cancer › Conclusion 5-1; Chapter Highlights, 1st bullet; Summary, 1st paragraph; Appendix B › Box B-3
evidence.extracted: The committee's graded conclusion 5-1 (quoted here) is its judgment. It rests on the pooled analysis; the cohort and the review are described in the Discussion. Box B-3 defines moderate as several findings from good- to fair-quality studies with very few or no credible opposing findings, where chance, bias and confounding cannot be ruled out. The Chapter 5 highlight goes further than the numbered conclusion (it says the evidence suggests that smoking cannabis does not increase the risk of lung and head and neck cancer in adults), and the Chapter 5 Summary words the conclusion as no statistically significant association. Beside the numbers, the grade is wider than the pooled interval allows: the interval (0.66 to 1.38) does not exclude a rise, the cohort hazard ratio is 2.12, and the Box B-3 definition asks for very few or no credible opposing findings; the chapter does not explain how these were weighed.

evidence.quote: moderate evidence of no statistical association between cannabis smoking and the incidence of lung cancer

evidence.locator: Chapter 5 › Research Gaps, bullets; Summary, 1st paragraph; paragraphs after Box 5-1
evidence.extracted: Chapter 5 gaps and summary: the committee judged the evidence on lung and head and neck cancer moderate for no statistically significant association; it lists small samples, low participation, unverifiable self-reported use and difficulty controlling confounders (family history, occupational exposures and diet often not accounted for) as common problems, says the long incubation of cancer needs long observation, and asks for studies that confirm the existing evidence on lung and head and neck cancers and for replication, because exposures are changing and many associations rest on single studies.

evidence.locator: Appendix B › Literature Search, 1st to 9th paragraphs; Search Strategies (Search 2); Primary Literature: Identification and Quality Review, 3rd paragraph; Data Synthesis and Strength of Evidence Assessment, 1st paragraph; Box B-2; Box B-3; Discussion, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: Method, search: six searches of Medline, Embase and the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews (PsycINFO for Search 4) covering January 1999 to 2 August 2016; Searches 2 to 6 were combined into a master library of 10,759 unique articles (1,488 first categorised as systematic reviews), sorted into 11 endpoint areas; filtering to the chosen endpoints left 6,540 primary articles and 288 systematic reviews. The Search 2 listing limits to English-language human studies from 1999. Method, appraisal: possible systematic reviews were screened with six questions, then rated good, fair or poor on five attributes adapted from the Cochrane group by at least two members independently (disagreements settled by deliberation or a third member); only good or fair reviews informed the report. Primary studies were reviewed guided by the Cochrane tool for randomised trials and the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale for cohort and case-control studies. The report says the committee was not tasked to conduct a systematic review and that literature may have been missed. Method, wording of conclusions: evidence was privileged in the order randomised trials, non-randomised controlled trials, prospective controlled studies, case-control studies, with case series only when nothing better; the committee notes that this order does not imply the size of an observed effect. The weight of evidence was decided in private deliberations of committee subgroups. Box B-3 defines substantial (several supportive findings from good-quality studies, very few or no credible opposing findings), moderate (several from good- to fair-quality studies, very few or no credible opposing findings; limitations including chance, bias and confounding cannot be ruled out), limited (fair-quality studies or mixed findings with most favouring one conclusion; significant uncertainty) and no or insufficient (mixed findings, a single poor study, or not studied).
evidence.source_read: NCBI Bookshelf full text (Chapter 7; Chapter 5 lung cancer and head and neck cancer parts; Appendix B)

evidence.locator: An Urgent Call for Change in Cannabis Research › Complications of cannabis research, 3rd paragraph
evidence.extracted: Tobacco and other co-occurring use: about 70% of people who use cannabis also smoke tobacco and cannabis is often combined with tobacco in cannabis cigarettes (reference 33, a 2016 review); statistically controlling for tobacco use can potentially remove valuable variance associated with cannabis use, which raises the question of how to balance specificity with generalisability; the same problem holds for ADHD, depression and anxiety. The authors suggest control groups with specific comorbidities and longitudinal extensions of existing studies.

evidence.locator: Report Overview › Goal and conclusions, Table 1 (Cancer row)
evidence.extracted: Table 1 sets the report's conclusions beside the WHO report's. Respiratory rows: bronchitis and respiratory symptoms (substantial for increased incidence and severity in people who have smoked cannabis long term; moderate for improvement after cessation), pulmonary function (moderate for acute but not chronic bronchodilatation; moderate for higher lung volume), COPD (limited in people who smoke cannabis occasionally, controlled for tobacco; insufficient for COPD severity), asthma (no or insufficient). Cancer rows: lung and head and neck cancers moderate evidence for no association, against WHO's statement that a cannabis and tobacco mix may increase cancer risk and that the effect of cannabis alone is unknown. Table 1 words the committee's cancer conclusion without the word statistical; the WHO report was not read, so the WHO statement is known only through this table.

risk_of_bias.note: Not appraisable here: the claim is seen only through the committee's account (a narrative review) and a commentary; the pooled analysis and the Swedish cohort were not read (METHODS §6.3). The limits the committee names: self-reported exposure without biological confirmation; no account of smoking technique or of the cannabis smoked; in the cohort, no follow-up of cannabis or tobacco use after conscription, unknown mixing of tobacco and cannabis and non-anonymous self-reports.

inconsistency.note: The pooled null result (0.96, 0.66–1.38) and the cohort's hazard ratio of 2.12 point different ways, and the committee does not show how the two were weighed; the sources differ in design, exposure definition and timing, which may explain part of it.

indirectness.note: Second-hand reading; exposure definitions differ between the two sources (at least 1 joint-year; more than 50 uses at conscription); the outcome is incidence of lung cancer in the studies' populations, with self-reported past use.

imprecision.note: The pooled interval (0.66–1.38) and, among people who did not smoke tobacco, 0.51–2.08 include no difference and a rise; the adenocarcinoma intervals (0.75–4.00; 0.85–3.56) are wide; few people with heavy long-term smoking.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable: four of the six pooled studies are unpublished, which reduces the risk of missing studies, but the pooled analysis was not read.

dose_response.note: Risk rose with duration and intensity in the pooled analysis, but not significantly; not counted.

grade.reasoning: Observational (case-control studies and one cohort), so the claim starts low. It rests only on the National Academies committee's account, a narrative review, with a 2018 commentary: the pooled analysis and the Swedish cohort were not read, so the figures are second-hand and the risk of bias cannot be appraised (METHODS §6.3: downgraded for risk of bias and indirectness). Risk of bias −1, inconsistency −1, indirectness −1 and imprecision −1 pass the floor, so the certainty is very low; any two would give the same. The relation is insufficient evidence (METHODS §6.1): neither an effect nor its absence can be shown with precision, because the pooled interval does not exclude a rise of 38% (and, among people who did not smoke tobacco, an odds ratio of 2.08) and a cohort points up. The committee's grade, moderate evidence of no statistical association, is its own judgment and concerns statistical significance; the editors do not adopt it as a finding of no effect (METHODS §6.3: no detectable effect needs precision). Not rated as 'causes': every source is observational and none can show cause. The status is mixed (a pooled null and a cohort that points up, not reconciled by the committee). The claim rests on narrative-review accounts only, so it stays at draft.

verification.flag_note: Section 7 draft for the senior author (decision p-ways-of-taking); findings only, no advice. Rests only on the National Academies report (Chapter 5 lung cancer section, Chapter 5 gaps and summary, Appendix B; read in full text on NCBI Bookshelf) and the Cousijn commentary, which are narrative reviews, so every number is second-hand and the claim stays draft and out of the at-a-glance box (METHODS §6.3). Callaghan et al. (2013), the Swedish conscript cohort followed 40 years (reference callaghan_2013), is not yet readable and will be added: it is the paper behind the only hazard ratio here, and its absolute numbers, exposure definition and handling of tobacco should replace the committee's account when it is read. Not read and without a reference record: Zhang et al. 2015, the pooled analysis (DOI 10.1002/ijc.29036) and Huang et al. 2015, the epidemiologic review (DOI 10.1158/1055-9965.EPI-14-1026). The relation insufficient-evidence and the certainty very low are the editors' reading under METHODS §6.1 and §6.3, not the committee's: its grade concerns statistical significance over a pooled interval that does not exclude a rise, with a cohort pointing up, and its chapter highlight is stronger than its numbered conclusion; the senior author may prefer contested, with a debate box, once the cohort paper is read. Cousijn's table drops the word statistical from the committee's cancer conclusion, and its criticism of a 500-participant cut-off was not found in the chapters read, so the commentary is used only for the tobacco co-use point and the WHO contrast (the WHO report was not read). Head and neck cancer (Conclusion 5-2) was read and is on the study card, not in this claim. No industry sponsor of the report is listed; the funding of the primary studies is not known here. The simple line gives no amounts.
